12.title: The Future of Data Systems
12.second_ed: Ch 13-14 (split: Streaming Philosophy / Doing the Right Thing)

thinking-about-data-systems.title: Thinking About Data Systems
thinking-about-data-systems.definition: Databases, caches, queues, and indexes blur together and get composed by application code — which then owns the guarantees; you become a data system designer.

reliability.title: Reliability
reliability.definition: Continuing to work correctly even when things go wrong; fault (component deviates) ≠ failure (system stops serving users) — design fault tolerance so faults don't become failures.

hardware-faults.title: Hardware Faults
hardware-faults.definition: Random, uncorrelated faults (10k disks ⇒ ~1 dead/day); answered first by hardware redundancy, increasingly by software fault tolerance that survives whole-machine loss (enabling rolling upgrades).

software-errors.title: Software Errors
software-errors.definition: Systematic, correlated faults — a bug hits every node at once, runaway processes, cascading failures — dormant until an environmental assumption breaks; no quick fix, many small disciplines.

human-errors.title: Human Errors
human-errors.definition: Operator configuration mistakes are the leading cause of outages; mitigate with good abstractions, sandboxes, thorough testing, fast rollback and gradual rollout, telemetry, training.

how-important-is-reliability.title: How Important Is Reliability?
how-important-is-reliability.definition: Reliability matters beyond critical systems (lost revenue, legal risk, users' irreplaceable data); trade it away only consciously, e.g. for a prototype.

scalability.title: Scalability
scalability.definition: A system's ability to cope with increased load — not a label but a set of options: 'if load grows this way, what can we do?'

describing-load.title: Describing Load
describing-load.definition: Load parameters chosen for your architecture (req/s, read/write ratio, fan-out…); Twitter's timeline fan-out shows trading read-time work for write-time work and averages hiding long tails.

describing-performance.title: Describing Performance
describing-performance.definition: Throughput for batch, response time for online systems — as a distribution: use percentiles (p50, p95, p99, p999), not means; tail latency amplification; measure client-side; add histograms.

approaches-for-coping-with-load.title: Approaches for Coping with Load
approaches-for-coping-with-load.definition: Rethink architecture per order of magnitude; scale up vs scale out (shared-nothing) pragmatically; elastic vs manual; stateless easy, stateful hard; no magic scaling sauce.

maintainability.title: Maintainability
maintainability.definition: Most software cost is maintenance; design for operability, simplicity, and evolvability to avoid creating legacy systems.

operability-making-life-easy-for-operati.title: Operability: Making Life Easy for Operations
operability-making-life-easy-for-operati.definition: Make routine operations easy: visibility/monitoring, automation, no single-machine dependence, clear operational model, good defaults with overrides, predictable behavior.

simplicity-managing-complexity.title: Simplicity: Managing Complexity
simplicity-managing-complexity.definition: Remove accidental complexity (from the implementation, not the problem) via good abstractions — SQL and high-level languages as exemplars; avoid the big ball of mud.

evolvability-making-change-easy.title: Evolvability: Making Change Easy
evolvability-making-change-easy.definition: Agility at the data-system level: how easily requirements changes can be absorbed; follows from simplicity and good abstractions.

relational-model-versus-document-model.title: Relational Model Versus Document Model
relational-model-versus-document-model.definition: Codd's relations of tuples with joins vs JSON-shaped self-contained documents; the choice hinges on the shape of your relationships (trees vs many-to-many).

the-birth-of-nosql.title: The Birth of NoSQL
the-birth-of-nosql.definition: A 2009 hashtag turned movement: driven by scalability, open source, specialized queries, and schema frustration; the likely outcome is polyglot persistence, not replacement.

the-object-relational-mismatch.title: The Object-Relational Mismatch
the-object-relational-mismatch.definition: The impedance mismatch between application objects and tables/rows; ORMs reduce boilerplate, documents reduce the gap for tree-shaped data like a résumé.

many-to-one-and-many-to-many-relationshi.title: Many-to-One and Many-to-Many Relationships
many-to-one-and-many-to-many-relationshi.definition: Store meaningful text once and refer by an ID that never changes (normalization); many-to-one/many-to-many need joins, which document databases support poorly.

are-document-databases-repeating-history.title: Are Document Databases Repeating History?
are-document-databases-repeating-history.definition: IMS's hierarchical model ≈ documents; CODASYL's network model used hand-navigated pointer access paths; the relational model won with the automatic query optimizer; documents nest like IMS but reference by ID like relational.

relational-versus-document-databases-tod.title: Relational Versus Document Databases Today
relational-versus-document-databases-tod.definition: Documents: schema flexibility, locality, closeness to app objects. Relational: joins and many-to-many. Schema-on-read vs schema-on-write; locality only pays when you need most of the document; the models are converging.

query-languages-for-data.title: Query Languages for Data
query-languages-for-data.definition: Declarative (SQL, relational algebra) states the result pattern and leaves the how to the optimizer — concise, implementation-hiding, parallelizable; imperative fixes order and steps.

declarative-queries-on-the-web.title: Declarative Queries on the Web
declarative-queries-on-the-web.definition: CSS selectors vs imperative DOM manipulation show the same advantages as SQL over CODASYL cursors: automatic un-application and vendor optimizations without rewriting code.

mapreduce-querying.title: MapReduce Querying
mapreduce-querying.definition: Map emits key–value pairs, the framework groups by key, reduce folds each group; functions must be pure. Two coordinated functions are harder than one query, so MongoDB added the declarative aggregation pipeline.

graph-like-data-models.title: Graph-Like Data Models
graph-like-data-models.definition: Vertices and edges for data where anything may relate to anything; homogeneous (social, web, road) or heterogeneous (Facebook's single graph); property graphs and triple-stores.

property-graphs.title: Property Graphs
property-graphs.definition: Vertices (id, in/out edges, properties) and edges (id, tail, head, label, properties); any vertex connects to any other; efficient traversal both ways; labels keep one graph clean; good for evolvability.

the-cypher-query-language.title: The Cypher Query Language
the-cypher-query-language.definition: Neo4j's declarative property-graph language: arrow patterns in MATCH, variable-length paths with *0.., optimizer chooses forward or backward execution.

graph-queries-in-sql.title: Graph Queries in SQL
graph-queries-in-sql.definition: Variable-length traversals need recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE) — ~29 lines to Cypher's 4; data models fit different uses.

triple-stores-and-sparql.title: Triple-Stores and SPARQL
triple-stores-and-sparql.definition: Everything as (subject, predicate, object): literal objects are properties, vertex objects are edges. Turtle/RDF syntax, the semantic web's overhyped history, and SPARQL's property paths.

the-foundation-datalog.title: The Foundation: Datalog
the-foundation-datalog.definition: predicate(subject, object) facts plus rules that derive new predicates, recursively; the academic foundation later graph languages build on (Datomic, Cascalog); rules compose and reuse.

data-structures-that-power-your-database.title: Data Structures That Power Your Database
data-structures-that-power-your-database.definition: Why storage engines exist: logs make writes cheap, indexes make reads cheap, and every index taxes writes.

hash-indexes.title: Hash Indexes
hash-indexes.definition: In-memory hash map from every key to its byte offset in an append-only log (Bitcask); fast, but keys must fit in RAM and range queries don't work.

sstables-and-lsm-trees.title: SSTables and LSM-Trees
sstables-and-lsm-trees.definition: Sorted segment files (SSTables) fed by an in-memory memtable + WAL, merged by background compaction — the LSM-tree design behind LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase.

b-trees.title: B-Trees
b-trees.definition: The ubiquitous update-in-place index: fixed-size 4KB pages in a balanced tree, O(log n) lookups, page splits on overflow, WAL for crash safety.

comparing-b-trees-and-lsm-trees.title: Comparing B-Trees and LSM-Trees
comparing-b-trees-and-lsm-trees.definition: LSM: faster writes, better compression, compaction risk; B-tree: steadier reads, one copy per key (good for transactional locks). Write amplification is the shared currency; measure your workload.

other-indexing-structures.title: Other Indexing Structures
other-indexing-structures.definition: Secondary indexes; heap files vs clustered vs covering indexes; concatenated and multi-dimensional (R-tree) indexes; fuzzy/full-text search.

transaction-processing-or-analytics.title: Transaction Processing or Analytics?
transaction-processing-or-analytics.definition: OLTP (few records by key, seek-bound, user-facing) vs OLAP (scan millions, bandwidth-bound, analyst-facing) — the fork that splits storage engine design.

data-warehousing.title: Data Warehousing
data-warehousing.definition: A separate read-only analytics database fed from OLTP systems by ETL, so analysts can scan freely without hurting production.

stars-and-snowflakes-schemas-for-analyti.title: Stars and Snowflakes: Schemas for Analytics
stars-and-snowflakes-schemas-for-analyti.definition: Star schema: a huge fact table (one row per event) with foreign keys to dimension tables (who/what/where/when/why); snowflake = normalized dimensions.

column-oriented-storage.title: Column-Oriented Storage
column-oriented-storage.definition: Store each column in its own file (same row order everywhere): queries read only the columns they use, and repetitive columns compress brilliantly.

column-compression.title: Column Compression
column-compression.definition: Bitmap encoding (one bitmap per distinct value) + run-length encoding; WHERE clauses become bitwise AND/OR; feeds vectorized, CPU-cache-friendly execution.

sort-order-in-column-storage.title: Sort Order in Column Storage
sort-order-in-column-storage.definition: Rows sort as units (position = identity); the first sort key doubles as an index and a compression multiplier; replicas can each use a different sort order (Vertica).

writing-to-column-oriented-storage.title: Writing to Column-Oriented Storage
writing-to-column-oriented-storage.definition: Update-in-place is impossible against compressed sorted columns — so writes go through an LSM-style in-memory buffer merged into new column files in bulk.

aggregation-data-cubes-and-materialized-.title: Aggregation: Data Cubes and Materialized Views
aggregation-data-cubes-and-materialized-.definition: Materialized views physically cache query results; data cubes precompute aggregate grids by dimension — instant for anticipated queries, inflexible beyond them.

formats-for-encoding-data.title: Formats for Encoding Data
formats-for-encoding-data.definition: Encoding (memory → bytes) and decoding (bytes → memory), and how each format handles schema change so old and new code can coexist through rolling upgrades.

language-specific-formats.title: Language-Specific Formats
language-specific-formats.definition: Built-in serializers (Java Serializable, pickle, Marshal): convenient but language-locked, insecure (arbitrary class instantiation → RCE), unversioned, inefficient — transient use only.

json-xml-and-binary-variants.title: JSON, XML, and Binary Variants
json-xml-and-binary-variants.definition: Textual interchange formats: vague numbers (JSON's 2^53 problem), no binary strings, optional heavyweight schemas; binary-JSON variants (MessagePack) save little because field names stay embedded.

thrift-and-protocol-buffers.title: Thrift and Protocol Buffers
thrift-and-protocol-buffers.definition: Schema-required binary encodings with code generation; field tags replace names; varints pack integers; evolution: never change tags, add only optional/default fields, never reuse removed tags.

avro.title: Avro
avro.definition: No tags or types in the bytes; reader resolves the writer's schema against its own by field name (reorder, skip unknown, default missing); writer's schema via file header, version + registry, or connection negotiation; friendly to dynamically generated schemas.

the-merits-of-schemas.title: The Merits of Schemas
the-merits-of-schemas.definition: Schema-driven binary encodings are compact, self-documenting (the schema can't go stale), checkable for compatibility before deployment, and support code generation — schema-on-read flexibility with guarantees.

modes-of-dataflow.title: Modes of Dataflow
modes-of-dataflow.definition: Who encodes and who decodes: through databases (writer → later reader), through services (client request / server response), through asynchronous message passing (producer → broker → consumers).

dataflow-through-databases.title: Dataflow Through Databases
dataflow-through-databases.definition: A message to your future self; needs backward and forward compatibility; beware old code round-tripping records and dropping unknown fields; data outlives code, so schema evolution unifies many eras; archive dumps re-encode consistently.

dataflow-through-services-rest-and-rpc.title: Dataflow Through Services: REST and RPC
dataflow-through-services-rest-and-rpc.definition: REST vs SOAP; why RPC's location transparency fails (lost messages, retry duplication needing idempotence, timeouts, variable latency, cross-language encoding); modern RPC (gRPC, futures, streams); servers-first ⇒ backward compat on requests, forward on responses; long-lived API versioning.

message-passing-dataflow.title: Message-Passing Dataflow
message-passing-dataflow.definition: Message brokers buffer, redeliver, decouple, fan out, hide addresses — one-way and asynchronous; any encoding but bidirectional compatibility gives deployment freedom; distributed actor frameworks (Akka, Orleans, Erlang) and their rolling-upgrade caveats.

leaders-and-followers.title: Leaders and Followers
leaders-and-followers.definition: One replica (the leader) accepts all writes and streams a replication log to followers, which apply writes in the same order; reads may go to any replica (active/passive, master–slave).

synchronous-versus-asynchronous-replicat.title: Synchronous Versus Asynchronous Replication
synchronous-versus-asynchronous-replicat.definition: Whether the leader waits for a follower's acknowledgment before confirming a write; fully sync blocks on any follower outage, so practice is semi-synchronous (one sync follower) or fully async (risking loss of acknowledged writes).

setting-up-new-followers.title: Setting Up New Followers
setting-up-new-followers.definition: Take a consistent snapshot of the leader pinned to a replication-log position, copy it to the new node, then replay all changes since that position until the follower has caught up — no downtime.

handling-node-outages.title: Handling Node Outages
handling-node-outages.definition: Follower failure heals by catch-up from its local log; leader failure needs failover — detect via timeout, elect the most up-to-date follower, reconfigure clients — with hazards of discarded writes, split brain, and the timeout dilemma.

implementation-of-replication-logs.title: Implementation of Replication Logs
implementation-of-replication-logs.definition: Statement-based (nondeterminism problems), WAL shipping (exact but coupled to engine/version), logical row-based (decoupled, cross-version, parseable ⇒ change data capture), and trigger-based (flexible, costly).

problems-with-replication-lag.title: Problems with Replication Lag
problems-with-replication-lag.definition: Reads from asynchronous followers can be stale — eventual consistency with no bound on 'eventually' — producing read-your-writes, monotonic-read, and consistent-prefix anomalies.

reading-your-own-writes.title: Reading Your Own Writes
reading-your-own-writes.definition: Read-after-write consistency: a user always sees their own submissions; via leader reads for self-modified data, time windows after updates, or last-write timestamps that replicas must have caught up to.

monotonic-reads.title: Monotonic Reads
monotonic-reads.definition: A user never sees time go backward across successive reads (no older data after newer); achieved by pinning each user to one replica, e.g. by hash of user ID.

consistent-prefix-reads.title: Consistent Prefix Reads
consistent-prefix-reads.definition: Writes that happen in a certain order are seen in that order by all readers (causality); a problem in partitioned databases where partitions have no global write order.

solutions-for-replication-lag.title: Solutions for Replication Lag
solutions-for-replication-lag.definition: Design for how the app behaves if lag reaches minutes or hours; application-level fixes are complex and error-prone, which is what transactions exist to spare you.

multi-leader-replication.title: Multi-Leader Replication
multi-leader-replication.definition: More than one node accepts writes and forwards them to the others (master–master, active/active); each leader is also a follower of the rest; introduces write conflicts.

use-cases-for-multi-leader-replication.title: Use Cases for Multi-Leader Replication
use-cases-for-multi-leader-replication.definition: A leader per datacenter (local writes, tolerance of datacenter and WAN failures), clients with offline operation (every device a leader, e.g. calendar sync), and real-time collaborative editing.

handling-write-conflicts.title: Handling Write Conflicts
handling-write-conflicts.definition: Concurrent writes to the same record on different leaders are detected asynchronously and must be resolved convergently: avoid them, last-write-wins (lossy), merge, or preserve for application logic on write or on read; CRDTs/OT automate it.

multi-leader-replication-topologies.title: Multi-Leader Replication Topologies
multi-leader-replication-topologies.definition: Communication paths for propagating writes — circular, star, all-to-all; sparse topologies break on a node failure, dense ones let writes overtake each other, a causality problem needing version vectors.

leaderless-replication.title: Leaderless Replication
leaderless-replication.definition: Any replica accepts writes directly, with no leader enforcing order (Dynamo-style: Riak, Cassandra, Voldemort); clients write to and read from several nodes in parallel and reconcile by version.

writing-to-the-database-when-a-node-is-d.title: Writing to the Database When a Node Is Down
writing-to-the-database-when-a-node-is-d.definition: No failover: write to all n replicas and succeed on w acks; read from all and take the newest of r replies; stale replicas heal via read repair and anti-entropy; w + r > n guarantees overlap.

limitations-of-quorum-consistency.title: Limitations of Quorum Consistency
limitations-of-quorum-consistency.definition: Even with w + r > n, stale reads leak through sloppy quorums, concurrent writes, writes concurrent with reads, partial write failures, and restores from stale replicas — quorums tune probability, not guarantees; monitor staleness.

sloppy-quorums-and-hinted-handoff.title: Sloppy Quorums and Hinted Handoff
sloppy-quorums-and-hinted-handoff.definition: Accept writes on reachable non-home nodes when a quorum of home nodes can't be reached (durability, not a true quorum); hinted handoff later forwards them home.

detecting-concurrent-writes.title: Detecting Concurrent Writes
detecting-concurrent-writes.definition: Concurrency is causal (neither operation knows of the other), not temporal; LWW forces an order and loses data; version numbers per key (and version vectors per replica) keep concurrent siblings for the application to merge, with tombstones for deletions.

partitioning-and-replication.title: Partitioning and Replication
partitioning-and-replication.definition: Each record belongs to exactly one partition (shard/region/tablet/vnode), but partitions are usually replicated too; under leader-based replication every node leads some partitions and follows others — the two schemes are chosen independently.

partitioning-of-key-value-data.title: Partitioning of Key-Value Data
partitioning-of-key-value-data.definition: Deciding which records live on which nodes so data and query load spread evenly; unevenness is skew and an overloaded partition is a hot spot — random placement spreads data but makes every read ask every node.

partitioning-by-key-range.title: Partitioning by Key Range
partitioning-by-key-range.definition: Each partition owns a contiguous sorted range of keys with data-adapted boundaries (Bigtable, HBase, RethinkDB); cheap routing and efficient range scans, but sequential access patterns like timestamp keys create write hot spots.

partitioning-by-hash-of-key.title: Partitioning by Hash of Key
partitioning-by-hash-of-key.definition: A stable hash (MD5, FNV) maps skewed keys uniformly onto hash ranges owned by partitions; balances load but destroys key order so range queries hit all partitions — Cassandra's compound key hashes the first column and sorts by the rest.

skewed-workloads-and-relieving-hot-spots.title: Skewed Workloads and Relieving Hot Spots
skewed-workloads-and-relieving-hot-spots.definition: Hashing can't spread traffic to one identical key (a celebrity's ID); the application salts the key with a small random suffix across ~100 sub-keys, paying with fan-out reads and bookkeeping of which keys are split.

partitioning-and-secondary-indexes.title: Partitioning and Secondary Indexes
partitioning-and-secondary-indexes.definition: Secondary indexes search by value, not primary key, so they don't map onto partitions; two approaches — document-partitioned (local) and term-partitioned (global) — trade write cost against read cost.

partitioning-secondary-indexes-by-docume.title: Partitioning Secondary Indexes by Document
partitioning-secondary-indexes-by-docume.definition: Local index: each partition indexes only its own documents, so a write touches one partition but a read by indexed value must scatter/gather across all partitions with tail-latency amplification (MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud).

partitioning-secondary-indexes-by-term.title: Partitioning Secondary Indexes by Term
partitioning-secondary-indexes-by-term.definition: Global index partitioned by the indexed term (or its hash), so a read hits one index partition while a write fans out to several nodes — hence usually updated asynchronously (DynamoDB GSIs, Riak search, Oracle global indexes).

rebalancing-partitions.title: Rebalancing Partitions
rebalancing-partitions.definition: Moving load between nodes as data, throughput, or membership changes; must leave load fair, keep serving reads and writes meanwhile, and move no more data than necessary.

strategies-for-rebalancing.title: Strategies for Rebalancing
strategies-for-rebalancing.definition: hash mod N moves nearly everything (never do it); fixed number of partitions ≫ nodes and move whole partitions (Riak, Elasticsearch); dynamic split/merge at a size threshold (HBase, MongoDB); fixed partitions per node with random splits (Cassandra vnodes).

operations-automatic-or-manual-rebalanci.title: Operations: Automatic or Manual Rebalancing
operations-automatic-or-manual-rebalanci.definition: A gradient from fully automatic to fully manual; automation is convenient but, combined with timeout-based failure detection, can cascade (slow node declared dead → rebalance adds load) — many systems propose an assignment and let an operator commit it.

request-routing.title: Request Routing
request-routing.definition: Service discovery for partitions: clients contact any node which forwards (Cassandra, Riak via gossip), a partition-aware routing tier (mongos, Helix, moxi), or a partition-aware client; all need an agreed current partition→node map, usually kept in ZooKeeper.

parallel-query-execution.title: Parallel Query Execution
parallel-query-execution.definition: MPP analytic databases break a join/filter/aggregate query into stages and partitions executed in parallel across nodes, far beyond the single-key and scatter/gather queries most NoSQL stores route.
